new_statements.quote: Native Bisu syllables (as opposed to Daic loan words) have the canonical form C1 (C2) V T (C3), where C1 represents an obligatory initial consonant, C2 an optional second element in a consonant cluster, V an obligatory vowel, T an obligatory tone, and C3 an optional final consonant. Stress, a relatively minor component of Bisu phonology, does not affect syllable structure. [...] [§1.4.5, p. 36:] Bisu has three contrastive tones, low, mid, and high

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (UMI 9995952, 359 pp., MPG PuRe copy with ClearScan text layer) and re-rendered dissertation p. 32 = PDF p. 63 as an image. §1.4.1 Syllable structure reads, verbatim: "Native Bisu syllables (as opposed to Daic loan words) have the canonical form C1 (C2) V T (C3), where C1 represents an obligatory initial consonant, C2 and optional second element in a consonant cluster, V an obligatory vowel, T an obligatory tone, and C3 an optional final consonant. Stress, a relatively minor component of Bisu phonology, does not affect syllable structure." The only difference from the reported quote is "C2 and optional" (a typo in the original) vs the report's "C2 an optional". §1.4.5 Tone, p. 36 (PD…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bisu is a register-tone language (three level tones, low/mid/high, obligatory on every syllable). Stress exists but is called 'a relatively minor component' of the phonology and is said not to affect syllable structure; no rule for where word stress falls is given. The related evidence in Nishida 1973 (pp. 59-60) is that bound/subordinate morphemes after the main syllable are reduced ('weak utterances') in normal speech, which points to prominence on the main (root) syllable, but Nishida does not call this stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Daic (Thai) loans have different syllable canons and borrowed rising tones (Person 2000; Nishida 1973 p. 59).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level, based on the author's fieldwork on Doi Chomphuu / Doi Pui Bisu (Chiang Rai, Thailand) = bisu1244; not the Laomian (Lancang) side of the retired code. Person cites Vacharee 1987 (Mahidol MA) as the description containing Bisu 'stress patterns'.
new_statements.identity_note: bisu1247 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry, not a language: it is the retired ISO 639-3 code [bii] 'Bisu', split by change request 2007-092 (effective 2008-01-14) into Bisu [bzi] = bisu1244 (Thailand Bisu, incl. Laopin of Yunnan) and Laomian [lwm] = laom1237 (Lancang County, Yunnan). Glottolog lists zero descriptive references under bisu1247. The quoted statement (Person 2000) describes Doi Chomphuu/Doi Pui Bisu of Chiang Rai = bisu1244, whose audit folder already holds the same file; it should be catalogued under bisu1244, not under the retired code (census law: retired codes confer no identity).

sources.note: No stress statement for Bisu. Three level tonemes; p. 59 subordinate morphemes carry a specific tone in careful pronunciation but are 'weak utterances' in normal pronunciation; pp. 59-60 tone modulation of main syllable + bound morpheme. Caution: the primary/secondary/tertiary stress rules in the same volume text file belong to Hope's Lisu paper, not to Bisu.
